query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A nanolaminate spinel oxide coating deposited on the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will enable the in‐situ formation and stabilization of a lubricious protective interface during sliding, thereby suppressing friction and wear across the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An uncoated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy that exhibits acceptable sliding performance only at moderate temperatures but suffers from increased friction and accelerated wear at elevated temperatures due to oxidation and unstable surface phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a nanolaminate, thermally stable spinel oxide coating to the CoCrFeNi substrate.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests in ambient (oxidizing) atmosphere under defined loads, evaluated continuously as the temperature is increased from approximately 25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and retention of a self-adaptive, low-shear spinel oxide layer at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures the coating acts as a robust, adherent barrier; as temperature increases, controlled oxidation of the coating induces an in‐situ transition to a dense, lubricious spinel structure that minimizes contact between the substrate and counterface, thereby reducing friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline uncoated CoCrFeNi alloy, the coated material will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate over the entire temperature span, with marked improvements particularly at higher temperatures near 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix, which shows deterioration in wear and friction performance at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Operational testing conditions from 25 °C to 800 °C under standard sliding loads in an ambient, oxidizing environment.
generation.uncertainty: While prior reports indicate improved high-temperature behavior from in‐situ formed spinel oxides in related systems, uncertainties remain regarding the long-term adhesion, phase stability, and self-renewal of the nanolaminate coating across the full temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one group of CoCrFeNi substrates with the nanolaminate spinel oxide coating applied by a controlled deposition technique, and a control group of uncoated substrates. Subject both groups to identical reciprocating sliding wear tests under the same load and ambient conditions, incrementally raising the test temperature from 25 °C to 800 °C.
measurements: In-situ measurement of the coefficient of friction during sliding
Post-test wear rate analysis via mass loss or profilometry
Microstructural investigation of the wear tracks (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to assess the formation and stability of the spinel oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the uncoated controls over the entire temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. At 300 K and 600 K, the ordered lattice structure of the high entropy alloy coating material is basically the same, and thus its hardness is basically the same. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy alloy sliding wear showed that the unmodified CoCrFeNi (or similar) matrices perform acceptably only at moderate temperatures, while high-temperature sliding leads to oxidation or destabilization of the lubricious surface. Later work, as exemplified by PMC7515071 on an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 alloy, demonstrated that minor compositional modifications can induce the in‐situ formation of a protective spinel oxide phase during sliding at high temperatures, which significantly lowers the friction coefficient and wear rate. The trend has moved from relying on the intrinsic behavior of the unmodified alloy to engineering the surface response through phase formation that is activated by temperature. Despite these advances, the strategy of modifying the bulk alloy composition or relying on processing-induced microstructures has not yet delivered a robust, continuous lubricant behavior across the entire range from room temperature to 800 °C.
decision.unsolved: The remaining challenge is to maintain a self-adaptive, stable and lubricious surface state that is effective over a continuous temperature range. Bulk modifications or alloying strategies may improve high-temperature behavior but often compromise lower temperature performance or require additional process controls. The open question is how to induce and retain a protective, low shear strength interfacial layer throughout the full temperature window without further complicating the alloy’s composition.
decision.lever: Apply a nanolaminate, thermally stable spinel oxide coating onto the CoCrFeNi matrix
decision.why: Building on the observed benefits of in‐situ spinel phase formation in related HEAs at high temperature, this intervention directly targets the sliding interface. By depositing a finely tuned, adhesive oxide coating designed to morph into a lubricious, self-renewing spinel structure under sliding conditions, it promises to stabilize low friction and wear across the full temperature range. This approach bypasses bulk composition changes while leveraging surface engineering to control oxidation and phase formation under defined temperature, load, and environmental conditions.
